summary: Provides guidelines for evaluating the performance of IPv6 transition technologies that use encapsulation or translation. Dual-stack nodes can be tested using RFCs 2544 and 5180. It also includes a metric for load scalability.

plainLanguage.summary: Networks that carry both versions of IP need a box that converts or wraps the traffic. This document says how to put such a box on a test bench and measure it: how to generate the traffic, which frame sizes to use, how to time the delay, and how to push past the limit to see how it degrades.

questions: how to benchmark ipv6 transition technologies
dual dut vs single dut test setup
subtitle: How to measure the speed and the delay of the boxes that let old and new IP networks talk to each other.

tldr.problem: IPv6 is not backwards compatible, so the two worlds need a translation or tunnel between them, and operators need to know how much such a device costs in speed and delay before they deploy it.
tldr.mechanism: The document reuses the established benchmarking methods and adds the parts specific to transition devices: the kinds of setup needed for translating and tunnelling equipment, the frame sizes to use once the extra headers are added, and a way to measure what happens when the device is overloaded.
tldr.outcome: The result is a repeatable procedure for measuring throughput, latency, delay variation, loss, DNS64 performance and overload behaviour, so that different implementations can be compared on the same terms.

facts.label: Ethernet frame sizes to be used

today: RFC 8219 is an Informational document published in August 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on the benchmark methods in RFC 2544 and RFC 5180, and it requests no IANA action because the address ranges it uses are already reserved.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Transition Needs Its Own Benchmarks
sections.content:
The methodologies described in RFC 2544 and RFC 5180 help vendors and network operators analyze the performance of IPv4 and IPv6-capable network devices. The methodology in RFC 2544 is mostly IP version independent, while RFC 5180 contains complementary recommendations specific to IPv6. However, RFC 5180 does not cover IPv6 transition technologies.

IPv6 is not backwards compatible, which means that IPv4-only nodes cannot directly communicate with IPv6-only nodes, and IPv6 transition technologies have been proposed and implemented to solve this. The document presents benchmarking guidelines dedicated to those technologies, so that the tests can give feedback to developers and network operators going through the IPv6 transition process.

It also includes an approach to quantify performance when operating in overload. Overload scalability is defined as a system's ability to gracefully accommodate a greater number of flows than the maximum number of flows the Device Under Test can operate normally, and the approach taken is to quantify it by measuring the performance created by an excessive number of network flows and comparing that with the non-overloaded case.
sections.plainLanguage: There are already standard ways to measure a router or a switch. Those ways assume the device speaks one version of IP. A transition box is different, because it rewrites or wraps every packet, and that changes the sizes on the wire and adds work at each hop, so it needs its own test procedure.

sections.title: Four Ways to Build a Transition
sections.content:
Two of the basic transition technologies, dual IP layer and encapsulation, are presented in RFC 4213, and IPv4/IPv6 translation is presented in RFC 6144. Most transition technologies employ at least one variation of these mechanisms, and the document gives a generic classification that helps when choosing a test setup.

A production network transitioning to IPv6 can be seen as three domains: Domain A, which speaks one version of IP; a core domain, which speaks the other version or both; and Domain B, again in the first version. The transition technologies are then categorized by how the core domain is crossed. In the dual stack case, devices in the core domain implement both IP protocols. In the single translation case, the network is assumed to have only Domain A and the core domain, and IPvX packets are translated to IPvY at the edge between them. In the double translation case, the network has all three domains, with IPvX packets translated to IPvY at the first edge and translated back to IPvX at the second. In the encapsulation case, the network also has all three domains, with IPvX packets encapsulated into IPvY packets at the first edge and de-encapsulated at the second.

The performance of dual-stack technologies can be fully evaluated with the methods in RFC 2544 and RFC 5180, so the document focuses on the other three categories. A second axis of classification is the use of stateful or stateless mapping algorithms. Technologies that use stateful mapping, such as NAT64, create dynamic correlations between IP addresses, or between address, transport protocol and port tuples, which are stored in a state table, and the efficiency with which that table is managed can be an important performance indicator. Additional benchmarking tests are therefore recommended for stateful transition technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four shapes a transition network can take. The middle of the network can speak both versions, or the traffic can be rewritten on the way in, rewritten again on the way out, or wrapped in a tunnel and unwrapped at the far end. The document leaves out the case where the middle speaks both, because the existing methods already cover it.

sections.title: The Test Setup and the Traffic
sections.content:
The test environment setups recommended for benchmarking IPv6 transition technologies are very similar to those in Section 6 of RFC 2544. The tester setup options from RFC 2544 and RFC 5180 can be applied, but the Device Under Test setup options have to be explained in the context of the targeted categories. Although both single tester and sender/receiver setups are applicable, the single tester setup is used to describe the DUT options.

For single-translation technologies a single DUT setup should be used: the DUT translates IPvX packets into IPvY packets, and the tester should be configured to support both IPvX and IPvY. For encapsulation and double-translation technologies a dual DUT setup should be employed: the tester creates a flow of IPvX packets, the first DUT encapsulates or translates them into IPvY, and the second DUT de-encapsulates or translates them back to IPvX and forwards them to the tester. One limitation of the dual DUT setup is its inability to reflect asymmetries in behaviour between the two devices, so additional performance tests should be performed using the single DUT setup. For encapsulation technologies in the single DUT setup, the tester should be able to send IPvX packets already encapsulated as IPvY, in order to test the de-encapsulation efficiency.

Dynamic routing should be employed, but routing and management frames are unwanted background data that can affect the result, so the procedures in RFC 2544 for routing and management frames should be used.

The test traffic represents the experimental workload and is dedicated to unicast IP traffic; multicast is outside the scope. The frame sizes to be used over Ethernet are 64, 128, 256, 512, 768, 1024, 1280, 1518, 1522, 2048, 4096, 8192 and 9216 bytes. For the rest of the transition technologies, the frame overhead introduced by translation or encapsulation must be considered, because the process generates different frame sizes on different segments of the setup, and this has to be taken into account when calculating the maximum theoretical frame rates. To avoid frame loss from an MTU mismatch between the virtual interfaces and the physical network interface controllers, the larger MTU of the two should be set on all interfaces of the DUT and the tester, and the recommended value for the physical interfaces as well as the virtual ones is the minimum IPv6 MTU size of 1280 bytes plus the encapsulation or translation overhead.

All tests should be performed with bidirectional traffic, and because UDP is simple, UDP measurements offer a more reliable basis for comparison than other transport protocols, so UDP traffic should be employed. Since a transition technology could handle both native IPv6 traffic and translated or encapsulated traffic, four traffic setups are recommended: IPvX only, 90 percent IPvX with 10 percent native IPvY, 50 percent of each, and 10 percent IPvX with 90 percent native IPvY.
sections.plainLanguage: A single box is tested by putting the traffic generator on one side of it, and two boxes are tested by putting one on each side, because a tunnel has to be opened at both ends. The frame sizes have to account for the extra headers the device adds, otherwise the link will overflow. And the traffic is a mix of native and translated packets, because a real device handles both.

sections.title: The Measurements
sections.content:
Throughput is taken unmodified from Section 26.1 of RFC 2544, as are frame loss rate, back-to-back frames and system recovery, and reset is taken from RFC 6201. Latency gets a new procedure. The throughput for the DUT at each of the listed frame sizes is determined, and a stream of frames is sent at that rate to a specific destination for at least 120 seconds. Identifying tags are included in at least 500 frames after 60 seconds, and for each tagged frame the time it was fully transmitted and the time it was received must be recorded; the latency is the difference between the two. Two quantities are calculated from the results: the typical latency as the median of the tagged latencies, and the worst-case latency as the 99.9th percentile. The test must be repeated at least 20 times, with the reported value being the median of the recorded values.

For packet delay variation, the one-way delay of every frame in a stream of at least 60 seconds is measured, and the packet delay variation is the 99.9th percentile of those delays minus the minimum delay. The inter-packet delay variation is the difference between the one-way delay of a frame and that of the frame before it; because its nature makes a single number misleading, the report for each measurement should include the minimum, median and maximum. The test must be repeated at least 20 times and the median of the three values reported.

For stateful transition technologies, the tests for concurrent TCP connection capacity and maximum TCP connection establishment rate from RFC 3511 should also be performed, following that document's setup and parameters.

DNS resolution performance is measured for DNS64, which provides DNS support for single-translation technologies such as NAT64. The test traffic is a sequence of six messages: a query for the AAAA record of a domain name from the client, the same query from the DNS64 server to the authoritative server, an empty AAAA answer, a query for the A record, a valid A record answer, and the synthesized AAAA answer back to the client. The tester plays the role of both the DNS client and the authoritative DNS server. IPv6 must be used between the client and the DNS64 server, but either version may be used between the DNS64 server and the authoritative server.

The objective is to determine the maximum number of successfully processed DNS requests per second. Queries are sent at a specific rate and the replies that arrive within a timeout, whose default value is one second, and that are valid, containing an AAAA record, are counted. If as many replies are received as queries were sent, the rate is raised and the test rerun; otherwise the rate is reduced and the test rerun. Each trial should last at least 60 seconds, and no timeout higher than one second should be used. Two conditions have to be tested in combination: how many of the queried names are already cached, and how many of them have an AAAA record of their own. The test with nothing cached and no existing AAAA records is required, and the other combinations are optional. Before use, the tester must perform a self-test in which it is looped back without the DUT, and it should be able to answer AAAA record queries at twice the test rate plus a margin, within a quarter of the timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the measurements are taken straight from the standard method for network devices. Latency gets its own recipe, because the usual one is not precise enough: a long stream of packets is timed one by one, and the report gives both the middle value and the near-worst value. The DNS test counts how many name lookups per second the translator can still answer correctly, and it must be run against a tester that has proved it can keep up on its own.

sections.title: Measuring Overload Scalability
sections.content:
Scalability has often been discussed, but in the context of network devices a formal definition or measurement method had not been proposed. Overload scalability is defined here as the ability of each transition technology to accommodate network growth, and since poor scalability usually leads to poor performance, it is measured by quantifying the network performance degradation associated with an increased number of network flows.

The test setups from Section 4 are modified to create that growth. For single-translation technologies the growth is generated by increasing the number of network flows produced by the tester. For encapsulation and double-translation technologies a multi-flow setup is recommended: considering a multipoint-to-point scenario, where one of the edge nodes is designed to support more than one connecting device, the recommended setup is an n:1 design, where n is the number of client devices connected to the same server device. This setup helps quantify the scalability of the server device, but for the overload scalability of the client devices further recommendations are needed: for encapsulation technologies an m:n setup can be created, where m is the number of flows applied to the same client device and n the number of client devices connected to the same server device, and for translation-based technologies the client devices can be tested separately with n network flows using the single DUT setup.

Performance degradation with simultaneous load is measured by running the Section 7 tests first for one network flow, then repeating them for n flows started at the same time, and calculating the relative performance change. The formula differs by benchmark: for lower-is-better benchmarks such as latency, the change is computed as (Xn - X1) divided by X1, and for higher-is-better benchmarks such as throughput, as (X1 - Xn) divided by X1, both multiplied by 100. As a guideline for the maximum number of flows n, the value can be deduced by measuring the concurrent TCP connection capacity. The number of tested parallel flows must be clearly specified, and the degradation is expressed as a percentage.

The incremental variant starts the n flows one after another, each after a time t, extending the duration of each iteration by the time needed to start all of them, and the measurement for the first flow should be at least 60 seconds long. Intermediary degradation points for one quarter, one half and three quarters of n may also be performed, and the report should state the incremental step T, in seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: To see how a device behaves when it is too busy, the test runs the same measurements again with more traffic, and then compares the result with the single-flow case. The document gives the exact formula for that comparison, and says how many parallel flows to try, which is taken from the number of connections the device can hold.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Benchmarking activities as described in the document are limited to technology characterization using controlled stimuli in a laboratory environment, with dedicated address space and the constraints specified in the sections above. The benchmarking network topology is an independent test setup and must not be connected to devices that may forward the test traffic into a production network or misroute traffic to the test management network.

Benchmarking is performed on a black-box basis, relying solely on measurements observable external to the DUT or System Under Test. Special capabilities should not exist in the DUT or SUT specifically for benchmarking purposes, and any implications for network security arising from the DUT or SUT should be identical in the lab and in production networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The tests are run in a lab on a private address range, and the lab must not be wired to the production network in any way that could carry test traffic into it. The device is treated as a black box, measured only from the outside, and it must not contain special test hooks, because then the lab would be measuring something that does not exist in production.

items.title: Throughput and loss
items.text: Taken unmodified from the RFC 2544 method, along with back-to-back frames and system recovery.

items.title: Latency
items.text: A stream of at least 120 seconds, with at least 500 tagged frames after 60 seconds.

items.title: Two latency numbers
items.text: The typical latency is the median of the tagged results; the worst case is the 99.9th percentile.

items.title: Delay variation
items.text: PDV is the 99.9th percentile of one-way delay minus the minimum; IPDV is the difference between consecutive delays.

items.title: Repetitions
items.text: Each test is repeated at least 20 times, and the median of the results is reported.

items.title: DNS64
items.text: The maximum number of DNS requests answered per second, with a one second timeout.
